newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Sihanouk signals role in seeking peace.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Sihanouk signals role in seeking peace.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk has urged coup leader Hun Sen to bring about peace in the troubled country, but stopped short of criticising the powerful leader or following through on a threat to abdicate.

Political analysts in Phnom Penh said on Wednesday Sihanouk's statements indicated the monarch had decided to engage in peace efforts with the government despite frustration over recent violence and the ouster of his son, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
"He is asking the government to exercise restraint," said one Asian diplomat. "He's not turning his back on the government or the country."

Sihanouk has expressed dismay over Hun Sen's bloody July 6 overthrow of Ranariddh and said he still recognised his son as first prime minister, even though Foreign Minister Ung Huot has been appointed the job.

Sihanouk did not block Ung Huot's appointment last week, but he also did not approve it and later called Ung Huot a "puppet" of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and derided recent events in the capital as a "comedy".
On Monday Sihanouk said he was ready to give up the throne if he could be assured Hun Sen would not criticise him for doing so.

Political analysts in Phnom Penh said the king's critical comments and his offer to abdicate could be seen as a challenge to Hun Sen, who has long feared the widely revered king would give up the throne, enter politics and challenge him for power.

By withholding his stamp of approval for Hun Sen's government the king was gaining leverage ahead of his talks on Tuesday in Beijing with Hun Sen and Ung Huot, who had been expected to seek Sihanouk's blessing for their new administration.
The king's offer to abdicate, issued as Hun Sen and his delegation were leaving Phnom Penh for Beijing, was another bargaining strategy, a Cambodian political analyst said.
"His abdication threat was an early strategy used as a way in which he could seek influence and push for peace," the analyst said.
In a statement on the meeting released in Beijing on Wednesday, Sihanouk said his offer to abdicate had been refused by Hun Sen.
"This delegation -- in particular his excellency Hun Sen -- assured N. Sihanouk of its fidelity and its support for the king whose offer to abdicate it did not accept," Sihanouk said.
In an earlier statement, Sihanouk said he had asked Hun Sen to end the violence in Cambodia and called for the country's constitution and human rights to be respected.
"The king still seems to have a strong belief in a real, genuine national reconciliation and peace. He's spelling that out," the Cambodian analyst said.
A statement from the government said the king had also said he would continue working on behalf of the people of Cambodia.

It said that Sihanouk, who has been receiving medical treatment in Beijing since February, would return to Cambodia soon to hold a religious ceremony for peace and national reconciliation in Siem Reap, home to the Angkor temple complex.

But while Sihanouk was willing to promote peace, he seemed unwilling to stand up to Hun Sen, analysts said. The king would not abdicate without his approval and has not blocked his government, they noted.
"This (talk of peace) is all pretty bland stuff," said a foreign political analyst.

"The king is uncomfortable that so much is riding on him now. The international community is looking to him, and he doesn't want to bless this government. But he doesn't want to stand in the way of Hun Sen," the analyst said. "I don't know what he can do to solve that situation."
